disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Bipolar Type) is characterized by a combination of mood episodes meeting criteria for mania or hypomania (often with depressive episodes as well) alongside psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations. A defining feature is that psychotic symptoms persist for at least two weeks in the absence of a mood episode, distinguishing it from bipolar disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis occurs only during mood episodes. Over time, individuals may show fluctuations between prominent mood symptoms and more enduring psychotic experiences, often leading to significant social and occupational impairment. The course is typically chronic or episodic, and diagnosis requires careful longitudinal assessment to differentiate it from schizophrenia and primary mood disorders.

narrative.stressor: About a year before presentation, Angelica retired from her long-held curatorial role earlier than planned to help care for her aging mother, who had developed significant medical and cognitive issues. The abrupt loss of her structured museum work, combined with the emotionally demanding caregiving and frequent trips from Rockland County into the Bronx, gradually eroded the balance she maintained through art, yoga, and community engagement. Over roughly ten months, family and close friends noticed that her usual meticulous planning around exhibitions, travel, and community projects gave way to increasingly erratic decisions and strained interactions at cultural events, leading her to withdraw from docent duties. When she began missing yoga hikes, mismanaging her mother’s appointments, and arriving at community meetings in a highly driven, disorganized state that frightened colleagues, a concerned niece and a fellow museum docent persuaded her to see a psychiatrist after she became unable to reliably care for herself or her mother.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My thoughts jump all over the place and I can’t keep a straight line when I talk or plan anything anymore.”

narrative.stressor: Demetrios had recently transitioned from part-time work and community college classes into his first full-time junior accounting position, taking on tax-season overtime and process-automation projects to prove himself. The long hours, performance pressure, and isolation of spreadsheet-heavy work gradually displaced his hiking, art openings, and game nights, leaving him increasingly preoccupied with work and his ambition to eventually run a boutique CPA practice. Over the next ten months, his supervisor and coworkers noticed that his previously precise, calm demeanor became more erratic: he stayed late to tackle grandiose side projects no one had assigned, clashed with colleagues about "big ideas" for the firm, and his concentration on basic bookkeeping tasks deteriorated. When a series of confused, off-topic client emails and missed deadlines led to a formal performance review—and his parents also reported dramatic changes in his behavior at home—his employer suggested he seek an evaluation through the company’s employee assistance program, prompting psychiatric consultation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly revved up at work, taking on too many projects at once and I can’t slow my mind or my pace down.”

narrative.stressor: In the year leading up to presentation, Nicole and her husband experienced escalating marital tension over finances, her long warehouse shifts, and her push for a promotion to shift supervisor, which he felt would further reduce their time together. The conflict intensified after a series of arguments about her weekend boxing schedule and church commitments, and she increasingly poured herself into extra shifts and community activities rather than addressing problems at home. Over approximately ten months, her family and church friends observed that she became markedly less reliable—forgetting potlucks she’d organized, showing up to boxing and work in an unusually agitated, driven state, and reacting defensively when others questioned her decisions—leading to friction with coworkers and threats that she might lose her job. A particularly chaotic evening, when she left home after a heated argument and her husband had to call her sister and pastor to help calm the situation, led the family to bring her to the emergency department, where psychiatric services were consulted.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve been feeling wound up and on edge for months, like my mood is stuck on high and I’m snapping at everyone, even my own family.”
